summary.text: A curved mirror has a reflecting surface that bulges outward (convex) or is recessed inward (concave), usually shaped like part of a sphere.
Concave mirrors reflect light inward to one focal point and appear in telescopes, headlamps and make-up mirrors, while convex mirrors reflect light outwards.
A convex mirror always gives a smaller upright virtual image with a wide field of view, so it is used on cars, in shops and in hallways.

items.prompt: The passenger-side mirror on a car lets you see a wide stretch of road behind you, with everything looking smaller. Why is this kind of mirror used?

options.label: It is flat, so the image is true to life and easy to judge
It flips the image upside down so you see more road
It bulges outward, giving an upright, smaller image with a wider view
It concentrates light to a single point to look sharper

items.explain: A mirror that bulges outward gives an upright but diminished image and a wider field of view.

items.prompt: You try to project the reflection from a shop's security mirror onto a sheet of paper, and it never appears on the paper. Why?

options.label: The mirror is too small to send enough light
The image is virtual and lies behind the mirror's surface
Paper soaks up every bit of reflected light
The mirror is a flat piece of glass

items.explain: A convex mirror always forms a virtual image, which sits "inside" the mirror and cannot be projected on a screen.

items.prompt: A solar power plant needs to turn sunlight from a wide area into one intense spot of heat. Which mirror shape does the job?

options.label: A bowl-shaped mirror that curves inward
A dome-shaped mirror that bulges outward
A perfectly flat mirror laid on the ground
A distorting mirror with many bumps

items.explain: Concave mirrors collect light from a large area and focus it into a small spot, as in concentrated solar power.

items.prompt: Telescope makers often use parabolic mirrors instead of spherical ones to image distant stars. What problem do they avoid?

options.label: Starlight failing to reflect from curved surfaces at all
The image always coming out smaller than the object
Images that are always virtual and cannot be seen
A blurring flaw that round mirror shapes suffer from

items.explain: Spherical mirror systems suffer from spherical aberration, so reflecting telescopes that image distant objects use parabolic reflectors.

items.prompt: Round curved mirrors were a popular luxury in the 1400s, long before flawless flat mirrors. What helped make them common?

options.label: They were easier to make from blown glass than a perfectly flat one
They needed no metal coating on the back at all
They were the only type that could show a clear image
They were cut from the same crystal as ancient lenses

items.explain: With 15th-century technology it was easier to make a regular curved mirror from blown glass than a perfectly flat one.

items.prompt: You study your face in a make-up mirror and in a hallway safety mirror, moving closer and farther away. How do the two differ as you move?

options.label: Both always show the same enlarged copy of you
Only the hallway mirror's image type shifts with distance
Neither image changes however you move
Only the make-up mirror's image type shifts with distance

items.explain: Concave mirrors show different image types depending on distance, while a convex mirror always gives a smaller virtual image.
